references.text: Jesus gives the twelve disciples the same mission: to heal the sick and proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near, parallel to the sending out of the seventy(-two) in Luke 10.
When Jesus sent out the twelve, he commissioned them to proclaim the kingdom of God and heal the sick—the same dual mission as here in the sending out of the seventy(-two).
The next verse repeats the message that the kingdom of God has come near, but now as a judgment on the towns that reject the disciples.
John the Baptist proclaimed the same message: "The kingdom of heaven has come near!"—the central eschatological message that Jesus and the disciples continued.
Jesus began his public ministry by proclaiming: "The kingdom of heaven has come near." The disciples in Luke 10:9 proclaim the same message.
Mark's summary of Jesus' preaching: "The time is fulfilled, the kingdom of God has come near"—the same core message that the disciples are to proclaim.
The context for the sending out: Jesus sends out seventy(-two) disciples, two by two, to prepare the places where he himself would come.
Paul healed the sick on Malta, a continuation of the healing mission Jesus gave the disciples in connection with the proclamation of the kingdom of God.
Isaiah's prophecy that the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the lame shall leap—a messianic expectation fulfilled through the healings linked to the coming of the kingdom of God.
Jesus himself spoke to the crowds about the kingdom of God and healed those who needed it—the disciples repeat his pattern of preaching and healing.
Jesus says that if he drives out evil spirits by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon them—healing and the kingdom of God are inseparably linked.
Jesus declares that he was sent to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom of God—this is the very core mission that the disciples now share in.
